newsitem.title: USA: Minn. 'Price of Govt' program useful to budget - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Minn. 'Price of Govt' program useful to budget - S&P.

text.p: Minnesota's "Price of Government" program has proven useful for state budget development, but imposing strict compliance requirements could cause a negative impact on local entities, Standard & Poor's reported in its CreditWeek publication this week.
The five-year-old advisory program provides a framework for longterm planning by measuring the cost of all government services statewide as a percentage of average personal income, S&P noted.
In 1997, for example, the price has been set at 18.2 percent for state, local and public education services, S&P noted.

While the program sets no expenditure limits, required revenues for governmental services have been reduced over the last five years when measured relative to the state's personal income level, S&P said.

Its use at the local level can cause budgetary and political pressures as the greatest contributors to the index have been school districts and local governments, giving opponents valid concerns, S&P said.

"In most circumstances, Minnesota's cities, counties, and school district's rely heavily on property tax revenues as the largest source of operating funds and the largest, and only, source of potential revenue flexibility," S&P said.

The demand for mostly county-financed social services programs increases during economic downturns or softness, while the index itself would shrink during the same period with declining personal incomes, S&P said.
Rapidly growing school districts might exceed state revenue averages as well, S&P said.

"If the targets become too limiting on revenues, particularly for local units and school districts, or if the legislature imposes strict compliance requirements for the underlying municipalities, the program could begin to negatively impact local governments service delivery and revenue flexibility," S&P said.
